lead: A satellite range is a travel time times the speed of light, so every timing error is a range error: 1 ns is 30 cm. The errors come from the satellite clock and orbit, the ionosphere and troposphere, and reflections and noise at the receiver, and each has its own cure. Only a few universities teach this topic, so the chapter is short.
prereq: You need satellite navigation: GPS and NAVSTAR for pseudorange and the navigation message, and geometric concepts of navigation for the cut-angle idea behind DOP.

blocks.text: Each satellite carries atomic clocks (rubidium and caesium), stable to about one part in 10¹³ over a day. The control segment measures each clock and broadcasts a correction polynomial:
δt<sub>s</sub> = a<sub>f0</sub> + a<sub>f1</sub>(t − t<sub>oc</sub>) + a<sub>f2</sub>(t − t<sub>oc</sub>)²
blocks.where: δt<sub>s</sub> is the satellite clock offset in s; a<sub>f0</sub> is the offset (s), a<sub>f1</sub> the drift (s/s) and a<sub>f2</sub> the drift rate (s/s²) at the reference time t<sub>oc</sub>.

blocks.text: Relativity also moves the clock: weaker gravity makes it run fast and orbital speed makes it run slow, a net gain of about 38 µs a day, or 11.4 km of range. So the clock is set slightly low before launch (10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz), and the receiver adds a small term for the orbit's eccentricity.

Orbit (ephemeris) error is different: it is not subtracted from the range. The receiver uses the broadcast orbit to compute where the satellite was; the 1 to 2 m by which that position is wrong appears in the range along the line of sight.

The ionosphere holds free electrons from about 60 km to 1000 km. Its strength is the total electron content (TEC), the electrons in a 1 m² column along the path (1 TECU = 10¹⁶ electrons/m²). The code is delayed by

blocks.where: d<sub>I</sub> is the extra range in metres; TEC in electrons/m²; f is the carrier frequency in Hz. At 10 TECU on L1 this is 1.6 m; daytime values near solar maximum are many times larger.

blocks.text: Because dI depends on frequency, two frequencies remove it. The ionosphere-free combination ρIF = (f₁²ρ₁ − f₅²ρ₅) ÷ (f₁² − f₅²) cancels the first-order delay exactly. Single-frequency receivers use the broadcast Klobuchar model, which removes about half. Near the magnetic equator (southern India) and the poles, scintillation, rapid fading of the signal, can break lock.

sections.h3: The troposphere, local errors and the budget

blocks.text: The troposphere is the neutral air below the tropopause (about 9 km over the poles, 16 to 17 km over the tropics). Its delay is non-dispersive, the same on every frequency, so two frequencies cannot remove it. The zenith delay is about 2.5 m (about 2.3 m dry, the rest from water vapour). At elevation E the slant delay is about dT ≈ dz ÷ sin E; models (Saastamoinen, Hopfield) remove most of it.

Multipath (late reflected copies) adds about 1 to 5 m; receiver noise is smaller. The root-sum-square of all residual range errors is the user equivalent range error (UERE). Geometry multiplies it: horizontal error ≈ HDOP × UERE, vertical error ≈ VDOP × UERE.

examples.question: On L1 (1575.42 MHz) the ionospheric delay is 12.0 m. (a) Predict the delay on L5 (1176.45 MHz). (b) The zenith tropospheric delay is 2.5 m: find the slant delay at 10° elevation. (c) The remaining UERE is 5.0 m and HDOP is 1.8: find the horizontal error.
steps: (a) d ∝ 1/f², so d<sub>5</sub> = d<sub>1</sub> × (f₁/f₅)² = 12.0 × (1575.42 ÷ 1176.45)² = 12.0 × 1.7933 = 21.52 m. L5 is the lower frequency, so its delay is larger.
(b) d<sub>T</sub> = 2.5 ÷ sin 10° = 2.5 ÷ 0.1736 = 14.4 m. It is the same on L1 and L5, so dual frequency does nothing to it.
examples.answer: (a) 21.5 m on L5; the ionosphere-free combination of the two ranges cancels both. (b) 14.4 m, which needs a model. (c) 9.0 m horizontal (1-sigma).

traps: The 1/f² law is for the ionosphere only; the troposphere is non-dispersive, so L1/L5 does not remove it.
A lower frequency has a larger ionospheric delay: L5 gets more than L1, not less.

quiz.q: Which layer is dispersive, and how does its delay scale with frequency?
quiz.a: The ionosphere; its delay scales as 1/f². The troposphere is non-dispersive.

quiz.q: What is UERE, and how does it become a position error?
quiz.a: The user equivalent range error: the root-sum-square of all residual range errors. Multiplied by HDOP or VDOP it gives the horizontal or vertical position error.

quiz.q: Why is a GPS satellite clock set to 10.22999999543 MHz before launch?
quiz.a: Relativity makes the orbiting clock gain about 38 µs a day; set slightly low, it ticks at 10.23 MHz as seen from the ground.

quiz.q: Zenith ionospheric delay on L1 is 8.0 m. Find it on L5.
A dual-frequency receiver is used near the horizon. Which errors remain, and why?
quiz.a: The first-order ionosphere is removed. The troposphere remains and is largest at low elevation (14.4 m at 10° for a 2.5 m zenith delay), so it needs a model; multipath also grows near the horizon.

beyond: Not for the exam. SBAS such as GAGAN map TEC in real time and must guard against equatorial plasma bubbles. Search for equatorial scintillation.
